title: Why is a research team investigating neutrinos focused on Lake Superior?
excerpt: A research team is investigating neutrinos, looking for them in Lake Superior.
content:
GRAND RAPIDS, Mich. (WOOD) — A research team is investigating neutrinos, looking for them in Lake Superior.

The Neil Armstrong, a research vessel for the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution, recently made its first journey from its home in Massachusetts through the Great Lakes, bound for Minnesota.

The project, known as the Experimental Neutrino Detector, is led by experts at the University of Minnesota-Duluth, sponsored by the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, and partnered with the U.S. Department of Energy’s Office of Science, the Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory in Illinois and Brookhaven National Laboratory in New York.

Neutrinos are tiny, subatomic particles that are so hard to detect that they are often referred to as “ghost particles.” Alec Habig, a physics professor at UMD and lead researcher on the project, told Minnesota Public Radio that the particles are so small that they rarely interact with matter and pass through “most materials without leaving a trace.”

“There are a billion of them for every normal electron or proton that you’re used to. So (they are) the most numerous particles in the universe and we know the least about them,” Habig said.

Neutrinos are practically everywhere, but the research project is specifically targeting the lake near Duluth. The Fermilab outside of Chicago has used a particle accelerator since 2005 to generate the world’s largest neutrino beam.

The Fermilab beam was first aimed at Soudan Underground Laboratory in a decommissioned mine about 80 miles north of Duluth, studying how the dynamics of neutrinos change over distance and time. It is now aimed at a facility in Ash River, Minnesota. The beam cuts through western Lake Superior near Two Harbors, about 20 miles northeast of Duluth.

A WHOI crew has built and assembled five detector arrays that have been placed underwater to monitor for neutrinos. Fiberoptic cables connect the arrays to a temporary facility setup on shore near Two Harbors.

Habig explained that when neutrinos travel through water, they emit “faint flashes of blue light” when they collide with atoms. At night, under the water, the detector arrays can pick up those flashes and even differentiate neutrinos sent from the beam and neutrinos from other sources.

Researchers say they “don’t really know yet” what they’ll learn from the neutrinos. A DARPA spokesperson only referred to the study as another way to understand science so we can “prepare our nation for that new world.”
